abstracts.abstract: The proliferation of microservices in distributed environments has exposed fundamental limitations in traditional service composition paradigms, particularly regarding decentralized governance and adaptive orchestration under unpredictable workloads. This paper introduces the Intent-Driven Service Orchestration (IDSO) paradigm, a novel theoretical framework that reframes service composition as an autonomous intent fulfillment process rather than a predefined workflow execution. Under this paradigm, service orchestration emerges from declarative intent specifications that are dynamically decomposed, negotiated, and executed by autonomous service agents operating within a shared semantic space. We formalize the theoretical foundations of IDSO using alternating-time temporal logic extended with service capability modalities, establishing sound axioms for intent consistency, conflict resolution, and emergent composition. Our theoretical analysis proves that IDSO enables polynomial-time decidability for intent realizability in bounded environments, a significant theoretical advancement over the undecidability results established for traditional orchestration models. Furthermore, we derive conditions under which composed services exhibit provable properties including fault tolerance, temporal correctness, and quality preservation. The IDSO paradigm fundamentally shifts the abstraction level of services computing from implementation-centric composition toward intent-centric coordination, offering a theoretically grounded foundation for next-generation service-oriented architectures. This work contributes both a new theoretical framework and proof techniques applicable to the broader domain of autonomous service coordination.

Service-level agreement (SLA) compliance in cloud-based service compositions remains a critical challenge due to the inherent uncertainty in multi-tenant resource allocation and the complexity of enforcing temporal constraints across heterogeneous services. Existing SLA violation prediction models suffer from either excessive computational complexity that renders them impractical for real-time decision-making, or inadequate accuracy that leads to costly service disruptions. This paper presents a novel stochastic game-theoretic framework for SLA-aware service composition that significantly improves upon existing approaches through a principled integration of probabilistic contract theory with mechanism design. We formulate the SLA compliance problem as a multi-agent stochastic game where service providers and consumers engage in strategic interactions under incomplete information about resource availability and workload patterns. Our theoretical analysis establishes that the proposed framework admits a stationary equilibrium in mixed strategies under mild technical conditions, enabling efficient computation of optimal composition policies. We derive novel bounds on the price of anarchy for SLA violations and prove that our mechanism achieves at least 94% efficiency compared to the social optimum while guaranteeing individual rationality for participating services. Compared to state-of-the-art approaches, our framework reduces computational complexity from O(n³) to O(n log n) while improving prediction accuracy by 23% on standard benchmark datasets, representing a substantial theoretical and practical advancement for SLA governance in cloud services environments.

Contemporary service-oriented systems face unprecedented challenges in maintaining security guarantees while supporting dynamic service composition in edge-cloud hybrid environments. Traditional perimeter-based security models prove inadequate for microservices architectures where services frequently migrate across trust boundaries and composition patterns evolve dynamically. This paper introduces SecureFlow, a novel security architecture that implements a paradigm shift from perimeter defense to intent-based, zero-trust service protection. SecureFlow comprises three integrated components: (1) a distributed intent specification language that enables fine-grained security policies expressed at the service capability level rather than network level; (2) a policy enforcement substrate that leverages confidential computing primitives to establish hardware-attested trust domains dynamically formed around service compositions; and (3) an adaptive threat assessment engine that employs graph neural networks to detect anomalous composition patterns indicative of sophisticated attacks targeting service orchestration logic. The architecture introduces the concept of ephemeral security contexts that materialize and dissolve with service compositions, eliminating the static security perimeters that constrain traditional approaches. We implement SecureFlow as a production-ready framework supporting mainstream container orchestration platforms and evaluate its effectiveness through extensive experiments across diverse attack scenarios. Results demonstrate that SecureFlow successfully prevents 99.7% of studied attack vectors while introducing less than 3% latency overhead for typical composition scenarios. This work establishes a new paradigm for service security that is inherently aligned with the dynamic, composition-centric nature of modern services computing.

Service composition quality in distributed environments is fundamentally limited by the lack of effective mechanisms for capturing, reasoning about, and optimizing non-functional properties across heterogeneous service implementations. Existing approaches to quality-of-service (QoS) prediction for composite services either rely on simplistic linear models that fail to capture complex property interactions, or employ black-box machine learning techniques that lack interpretability and struggle with cold-start problems in dynamic service ecosystems. This paper presents QoSMaster, a comprehensive system for multi-dimensional service quality management that significantly advances the state of the art through a hierarchical Bayesian framework capable of learning fine-grained quality patterns across service, composition, and deployment dimensions. QoSMaster introduces a novel architecture comprising: (1) a semantic service quality model that captures functional and non-functional properties through hierarchical latent representations; (2) an adaptive composition optimizer that employs gradient-based search over the learned quality space to identify Pareto-optimal service combinations; and (3) a real-time quality monitor that detects and predicts performance degradation using stream processing techniques. We conduct extensive evaluation using production workloads from a major cloud platform, comparing QoSMaster against seven state-of-the-art approaches across multiple quality dimensions including response time, availability, cost, and user satisfaction. Results demonstrate that QoSMaster achieves 31% higher prediction accuracy for composition quality, reduces SLA violations by 47%, and improves overall composition efficiency by 28% compared to the best existing methods, representing substantial and measurable improvements for service composition quality in real-world deployments.
